rationale: The book's core identification of the pearl as the full moon (keseh) governing appointed times and serving as the one-pearl entry gate requires extensive retranslations of peninim, letter-play equating keseh with throne, wholesale re-renderings of Proverbs 3 and 31 as unstated moon portraits, and multi-step pattern chaining that go far beyond the texts. The common reading that the pearl is the kingdom of heaven (or its supreme-value equivalent) as the object worth selling all to obtain explains Matthew 13:45-46 and its immediate parallels with far fewer assumptions, directly from the parable's own wording and kingdom context, while still accommodating the OT value comparisons and Rev 21:21 glory imagery without contradiction.
book_core_identification: The pearl is the full moon (keseh, the night sky's one complete light), governor of the appointed times (moedim) and the one-pearl gates that constitute the merchant's entry at the King's gate.
book_secondary_elaborations: Wisdom and the virtuous bride are priced above pearls (peninim under KJV rubies) and function as the good merchandise sought by the merchant
Proverbs 3 and 31 poems re-rendered line-by-line as describing the moon's rising, circuit, appointed portions, and borrowed light without using any moon-word
Pearl properties (one, round, white, complete, water-born) and east-gate entry matched to full-moon phase and Ezekiel's new-moon gate
Keseh spelling identity with kisse' (throne) and covering-in-light versus dark counterfeit moon
Matt 7:6 swine-trampling applied to nations changing the times; calendar and enemy-contrast elaborations
strongest_counter_interpretation: The pearl primarily symbolizes the kingdom of heaven (and by extension salvation, Christ, or the gospel) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing value worth surrendering everything else to obtain, chiefly from the Parable of the Pearl of Great Price.
counter_core_identification: The pearl is the kingdom of heaven itself (or Christ/salvation) as the object of incomparable worth that one sells all to buy.
material_core_denial: The pearl does not identify the full moon, the appointed times, or a calendar gate of entry; it identifies the kingdom of heaven (or its supreme spiritual equivalent) of surpassing value.
counter_case: Matthew 13:45-46 explicitly likens the kingdom of heaven to a merchant who finds one pearl of great price and sells all to buy it, in immediate parallel with the treasure-in-the-field parable (13:44) whose treasure is the kingdom
Matthew 7:6 treats pearls as holy/precious things not to be cast before swine, naturally read as sacred truth or the gospel rather than lunar times
Revelation 21:21 places one-pearl gates among the precious materials of the New Jerusalem, reinforcing heavenly glory and access without requiring monthly full moons
Proverbs 3:15; 8:11; 31:10 and Job 28:18 price wisdom and the virtuous woman above pearls/rubies as statements of supreme spiritual value, not as equations of pearl with moon

No OT text calls the moon a pearl or equates peninim with keseh/full moon; the book's links are constructed via Strong's, spelling variants, and poetic re-reading rather than explicit or uniform patterns
book_explanatory_advantages: Recovers peninim (Strong's 'probably a pearl') under KJV rubies so that OT pricing of wisdom and bride can inform the parable's goodly pearls
Highlights the parable's 'one' pearl as complete/whole/round and matches it to the sky's single full moon plus each Rev 21 gate being of one pearl
Connects Ps 104:19 (moon for seasons), Ps 81:3 and Prov 7:20 (keseh), Job 26:9 (throne covering), and east-gate opening (Ezekiel) into a single calendar-gate reading
Supplies a uniform symbolic system in which the merchant buys entry rather than jewelry
counter_explanatory_advantages: Follows immediately from the wording and kingdom-parable context of Matthew 13 without any retranslation, letter-play, or poem re-rendering
Requires no extra assumptions about unstated moon portraits, throne/full-moon identity, or calendar mechanics
Accommodates both dominant (disciple seeks kingdom-pearl) and reverse (Christ seeks church-pearl) readings while remaining inside the parable
Explains Matt 7:6 simply as not profaning sacred things and Rev 21:21 as heavenly preciousness, both consistent with supreme-value symbolism
Matches the 'sells all' motif to standard discipleship commitment with fewer interpretive steps
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: The explicit structure of Matthew 13:45-46 (kingdom of heaven is like the merchant who finds and buys the pearl), which positions the pearl as the object of value corresponding to the kingdom itself (or the seeking of it); treating the pearl as a separate full-moon entry ticket forces an unstated addition that the kingdom equals the gate-system
The parallel treasure parable (Matt 13:44) in which the man sells all for the treasure that is the kingdom, leaving no textual room for substituting a full-moon calendar gate

The complete absence of any prior scriptural pattern that equates 'pearl' with 'full moon' or 'appointed times'; the moon is never called a pearl, so the identification cannot be derived by the book's own multi-witness standard without circular construction
decisive_sources: Matthew 13:45-46 together with the parallel treasure parable (13:44)
Revelation 21:21 in its New-Jerusalem precious-materials context
Proverbs 3:15; 8:11; 31:10 and Job 28:18 as pure value comparisons
unresolved_objections: Linguistic recovery of peninim as pearl is plausible and creates a real verbal link between the parable and the OT value statements
The uniqueness of the full moon as the sky's one complete white light and the 'one pearl' per gate supply a poetic correspondence if the overall method is granted
The book's closed-book OT derivation principle is applied consistently with its earlier sower-parable demonstration
